    ORIGINAL RESEARCH ARTICLE



The Effects of On‑Field Heat Index and Altitude on Concussion
Assessments and Recovery Among NCAA Athletes
Landon B. Lempke1 · Robert C. Lynall1 · Rachel K. Le1 · Michael McCrea2,3 · Thomas McAllister4 ·
Julianne D. Schmidt1 · CARE Consortium Investigators

Accepted: 21 November 2020
© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2020


Abstract
Background Recent literature has indicated altitude may be a protective factor for concussion but it is unknown whether
altitude or heat index affects recovery.
Objective To examine whether on-field heat index and altitude at the time of injury alter acute (< 48 h) concussion assess-
ments, days-to-asymptomatic, and days-to-return-to-play in collegiate athletes following concussion.
Methods Collegiate athletes (n = 187; age = 19.7 ± 1.4 years; male = 70.6%) underwent baseline assessments across 30
universities and experienced a concussion in this retrospective cohort study. Altitude (m) and heat index (°C) at the time
and location of injury were determined using valid online database tools. Acute concussion assessments included the Sport
Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) symptom inventory, Balance Error Scoring System (BESS), and the Immediate Post-
Concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing (ImPACT). We used multiple linear regression models to determine whether
heat index and altitude predicted each acute assessment outcome, days-to-asymptomatic, and days-to-return-to-play.
Results Collegiate athletes were concussed at a 181.1 m (range − 0.6 to 2201.9 m) median altitude and 17.8 °C (range − 6.1
to 35.6 °C) median heat index. Altitude did not predict (p ≥ 0.265) any outcomes. Every one-degree increase in heat index
reduced days-to-asymptomatic (p = 0.047; R2 = 0.06) and days-to-return-to-play (p = 0.006; R2 = 0.09) by 0.05 and 0.14 days,
respectively. Heat index and altitude did not explain significant variance in SCAT, BESS, and ImPACT composite scores
(p’s = 0.20–0.922).
Conclusion Our findings suggest that on-field altitude and heat index at the time of injury do not contribute to clinically
meaningful changes on acute assessments or concussion recovery. On-field altitude and heat index do not appear to signifi-
cantly alter assessment outcomes or clinical recovery, suggesting that environmental factors at altitudes below < 2500 m are
negligible outcomes for researchers and clinicians to consider post-concussion.

 "evidenceSummary": "The authors reviewed seven studies of anticipated direct head impacts (five in vivo, two computational) and three studies of visual and sensorimotor performance in American football and ice hockey players. In a youth ice hockey study (n = 16), anticipation of medium-intensity impacts reduced rotational head acceleration, but no protective effect was seen for severe impacts, and a high school American football study (n = 32) found no clear difference. Better visual-motor and oculomotor performance was associated with lower impact severity or frequency in a college football study (n = 38) and a high school ice hockey study (n = 12), but not in a high school football study (n = 37).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Most anticipation studies were laboratory or small single-team, single-season samples, and the computational models were not validated against live impacts. The visual performance evidence rests on three small studies that used arbitrary high and low performer cut-offs, and none is a controlled trial of vision training.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the review as showing that vision training reduces concussion risk, when the authors describe that evidence as preliminary and drawn from an uncontrolled study.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Kung SM, Suksreephaisan TK, Perry BG, Palmer BR, Page RA. The effects of anticipation and visual and sensory performance on concussion risk in sport: a review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2020;6:54.",
   "doi": "10.1186/s40798-020-00283-6",
   "abstract": "Reviews anticipation of head impacts and visual and sensorimotor performance as factors in sport-related concussion risk, and whether vision training may reduce concussion rates. Anticipation reduced head accelerations for mild-to-moderate impacts but less so for severe ones, and the evidence on visual performance is conflicting.",
   "tldr": "Anticipating a head impact may lower head acceleration for mild-to-moderate hits, but the benefit is inconsistent and does not clearly extend to severe impacts. Vision training looks promising for reducing concussion risk, but controlled evidence is lacking.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of studies published up to December 2019, identified through PubMed, SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE, Web of Science and CINAHL using search terms on head acceleration, vision training, anticipation and concussion, plus reference-list checks. It included studies of healthy participants on anticipation and head acceleration, and on visual and sensorimotor performance and concussion.",
   "findings": "Seven studies examined anticipation of direct impacts: five in vivo (samples of 9 to 32) and two computational. In youth ice hockey, anticipation reduced rotational acceleration for medium-intensity impacts but not severe ones, and linear acceleration was not clearly changed in most studies. Better visual performance was linked to lower head-impact severity or frequency in two of three studies.",
   "limitations": "Most included studies were small, single-team or laboratory studies, and the computational models were not checked against live impacts. The authors note the research area is in its infancy and that helmeted sports dominate the evidence.",
   "practicalImplications": "Anticipation and visual-motor training could be included as one part of a wider approach that also covers neck strength and protective positioning. Controlled trials are still needed before vision training is used to reduce concussion risk.",
   "athleteDev": "Vision and anticipation training may help athletes prepare for collisions, but the evidence is preliminary and the review does not show that such training reduces concussion in sport.",
   "rtp": "The review does not address return to sport after concussion and cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }

{
 "id": "Q74",
 "sourceFile": "The effects of cannabidiol oil on noninvasive measures of muscle damage in men.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The Effects of Cannabidiol Oil on Noninvasive Measures of Muscle Damage in Men' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Nutrition & Hydration"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Sports Medicine", "Nutrition"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Thirteen untrained men (mean age 21.85 years) completed a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial comparing 150 mg CBD oil with placebo oil, separated by a 2-week washout, after 6 sets of 10 maximal eccentric elbow-flexor contractions. Condition-by-time interactions and condition main effects were not significant for perceived soreness, arm circumference, hanging joint angle or peak torque (P > 0.05), while soreness rose and joint angle and RPE changed over time in both conditions.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample was small and untrained, with one dose (about 2 mg/kg per day) and only noninvasive markers, so the trial cannot rule out effects in trained athletes, at other doses or on blood markers of damage. The result is a null finding for this dose and schedule only.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the null result as proof that CBD does not aid recovery, when the authors tested one dose and schedule in untrained men.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2021,
   "citation": "Cochrane-Snyman KC, Cruz C, Morales J, Coles M. The effects of cannabidiol oil on noninvasive measures of muscle damage in men. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2021;53(7):1460-1472.",
   "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000002606",
   "abstract": "Investigated whether 150 mg CBD oil, compared with placebo, affects perceived soreness, arm circumference, joint angle, peak torque and RPE after eccentric elbow-flexor exercise in 13 untrained men. No condition effects or interactions were found, only time effects from the exercise-induced damage.",
   "tldr": "A moderate CBD dose taken after eccentric arm exercise did not reduce soreness, swelling, loss of range of motion or strength loss in untrained men compared with placebo. Exercise-induced muscle damage was confirmed by time effects in both groups.",
   "methods": "Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design in which 13 untrained men took 150 mg CBD (two 75 mg doses 8 h apart) or placebo on the exercise day and at 24 and 48 h, after 6 sets of 10 maximal eccentric elbow-flexor actions on an isokinetic dynamometer. Soreness, arm circumference, hanging joint angle, peak torque and RPE were measured before, after and at 24, 48 and 72 h.",
   "findings": "No condition-by-time interaction or condition main effect was significant for perceived soreness, arm circumference, joint angle or peak torque (all P > 0.05). Time effects were significant for soreness (P < 0.001, partial eta squared 0.71), joint angle (P = 0.006) and RPE (P = 0.004). Peak torque fell about 12% from pre- to post-exercise across conditions, but this was not statistically significant across all visits.",
   "limitations": "Only 13 untrained men were studied, with a single dose and schedule (about 2 mg/kg per day) and no blood markers of inflammation or muscle damage. The abstract describes four ANOVAs while the methods describe five (RPE included), and the age is given as 21 years in one place and 21.85 years in another.",
   "practicalImplications": "For untrained adults, this dose and schedule of CBD oil would not be expected to reduce soreness or strength loss after heavy eccentric work, so the evidence does not support using it as a recovery aid.",
   "athleteDev": "The study tested untrained men, so it does not apply directly to trained athletes. It gives no support for CBD as a performance-recovery aid at this dose.",
   "rtp": "The study does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }
}

input.content:
{
 "id": "Q75",
 "sourceFile": "The effects of electronic nicotine delivery systems on athletes.pdf",
 "decision": "DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "The article's own DOI is not printed in the text; the only DOI-like string is a reference-list link.",
 "doiMissing": true,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The Effects of Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems on Athletes' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Athlete Wellbeing",
 "domains": ["Athlete Wellbeing", "Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A narrative review of electronic nicotine delivery system (ENDS, or vaping) use in the general population and in athletes, with no search method described. The authors summarise cardiovascular, pulmonary and recovery effects, and the outbreak of severe vaping-associated lung injury, which they link mainly to THC-containing liquids (more than 805 cases and 12 deaths at the time of writing). They conclude that ENDS appear to have fewer performance-related and long-term health effects than tobacco cigarettes, but the long-term consequences remain unknown.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review has no search strategy, evidence grading or primary data, and athlete-specific evidence is very limited, so most conclusions are extrapolated from general-population and preclinical data.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 'fewer effects than cigarettes' conclusion as evidence that ENDS are safe for athletes, when the authors stress that long-term effects are unknown and athlete data are largely missing.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Young SE, Henderson CA, Couperus KS. The effects of electronic nicotine delivery systems on athletes. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2020;19(4):146-150.",
   "doi": "",
   "abstract": "Reviews the recent literature on electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS, or vaping) and athletes, covering cardiovascular, pulmonary and recovery effects and the severe lung injury linked to ENDS use. The effects appear less significant than those of smoking tobacco cigarettes, but the extent and longevity of the consequences are unclear.",
   "tldr": "Vaping appears to carry less cardiovascular and lung risk than smoking, but it still affects heart rate variability, airway function and sleep, and vaping-associated lung injury is a serious risk. The long-term effects on athletic performance are unknown.",
   "methods": "Narrative review with no described search strategy. It summarises ENDS prevalence, cardiovascular, pulmonary and recovery effects, and the 2019 outbreak of vaping-associated lung injury.",
   "findings": "Nicotine raises sympathetic activity, and habitual ENDS users showed reduced heart rate variability, as cigarette smokers do, with the effect seen only with nicotine-containing liquid. Pulmonary effects are smaller than those of tobacco smoke but not harmless, with daily adult users showing lower FEV1 in one study and users reporting up to a two-fold increase in bronchitis-type symptoms. Little data exist on ENDS effects on athletic strength, sprint or endurance performance.",
   "limitations": "No search method is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. Athlete-specific data are minimal, and the authors note that the long-term consequences are unknown.",
   "practicalImplications": "Athletes who use ENDS should be told about nicotine effects, the risk of lung injury (particularly with THC-containing liquids), and the unknown long-term effects. Explosion and burn injuries from devices are also a documented risk.",
   "athleteDev": "The review finds little evidence on how ENDS affect strength, sprint or endurance performance, so it cannot show whether ENDS use helps or harms athletic performance.",
   "rtp": "Preclinical studies show that nicotine impairs tendon and fracture healing, and the authors suggest ENDS nicotine may do the same by extrapolation. ENDS-specific injury-healing data are missing, so the review cannot guide return-to-sport decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q77",
 "sourceFile": "The effects of lower limb wearable resistance on sprint running performance - A systematic review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The effects of lower limb wearable resistance on sprint running performance: A systematic review' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Track & Field", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A systematic review (PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science, from inception to November 2018) of ten studies with 116 participants who sprinted with lower-limb wearable resistance (WR), ranging from untrained individuals to national-level athletes. Micro-loads of about 2 to 5% body mass increased contact time and reduced step frequency, and 5% loads slowed sprint times in two studies, while stride length was largely unchanged. One six-week study in untrained participants found no significant change in maximal sprinting speed.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Most included studies had 8 to 24 participants and single sessions, and the one training study used untrained participants with a single post-test. Several included studies were conference papers, and force production was not measured directly in most, so the claim that WR can improve sprinting is inferred from mechanics.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the conclusion that WR 'has the potential to elicit improved sprinting performance' as evidence of faster sprinting, when the authors infer this from kinematics and only one training study exists.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Feser EH, Macadam P, Cronin JB. The effects of lower limb wearable resistance on sprint running performance: a systematic review. European Journal of Sport Science. 2020;20(3):394-406.",
   "doi": "10.1080/17461391.2019.1629631",
   "abstract": "Systematic review of ten studies (116 participants) on lower-limb wearable resistance during sprint running. Micro-loads of 0.6 to 5% body mass increased contact time and reduced step frequency, slowed total sprint time in several studies, and one longitudinal study in untrained participants found no significant change in maximal sprinting speed.",
   "tldr": "Lower-limb wearable resistance of up to 5% body mass mainly changes sprint mechanics, increasing contact time and reducing step frequency, with stride length largely unchanged. Its effect on sprint performance is small and has been little studied in training.",
   "methods": "Systematic review following PRISMA guidance. PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science were searched from inception to November 2018 with Boolean terms for limb, sprint and resistance. Eligible studies measured acute kinematic, kinetic or performance effects, or longitudinal effects, of lower-limb wearable resistance in injury-free participants. Of 692 records, ten were included and effect sizes were calculated as Cohen's d.",
   "findings": "Eight studies measured acute kinematics. Loads of about 2 to 5% body mass on the thigh, shank or whole leg increased contact time (about 3 to 6%) and reduced step frequency (about 2 to 4%), while stride length was largely unchanged. In acute performance studies, 5% body-mass loading slowed sprint times by about 2 to 3% in two studies, while lighter loads did not significantly change total sprint times. The one six-week study of 5% ankle loading in untrained participants increased stride length and reduced stride frequency without a significant change in maximal speed.",
   "limitations": "The included studies were small and mostly single-session, and the training study had a single post-test, so the effects of off-loading are unknown. Force production was not measured directly in most studies, and no information on the start and acceleration phases was given for the training study.",
   "practicalImplications": "Coaches can use lower-limb loads of up to about 5% body mass to target step frequency and contact time in short sprint work. Loads should be progressed gradually because added rotational inertia may raise injury risk, and the review does not show that this improves sprint times.",
   "athleteDev": "Lower-limb wearable resistance can overload stride frequency and may encourage more horizontal force in acceleration work, with stride length unchanged. Its effect on sprint speed is not established.",
   "rtp": "The review includes only injury-free participants and does not study rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play loading decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q78",
 "sourceFile": "The effects of mental fatigue on sport-specific motor performance among team sport athletes - A systematic scoping review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The effects of mental fatigue on sport-specific motor performance among team sport athletes: A systematic scoping review' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Soccer", "Basketball", "Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Healthy Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A scoping review of 16 randomised controlled trials in healthy team-sport athletes, mostly soccer, in which a cognitively demanding task (most often a 30-minute Stroop task) was compared with a control before sport-specific tests. Mental fatigue impaired intermittent endurance (Yo-Yo IR1) and technical outputs such as errors, ball losses and passing or shooting accuracy in most studies, while total distance in some small-sided games was unchanged. Perceived exertion rose in most studies that measured it, while heart rate and blood lactate were largely unchanged.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Samples ranged from 9 to 48 participants, were mostly male, and were tested in laboratory or small-sided game settings, and the review mainly rested on exclusion of two low-quality studies rather than formal grading. The abstract reports 12 included studies, while the methods, results and Table 1 report 16, and the psychophysiological section cites 19 studies, so the study count should be checked against the full text.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the review as showing that mental fatigue reliably impairs match performance, when the evidence comes from short induced-fatigue tests in small samples and game-based distance results were often null.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Yuan R, Sun H, Soh KG, Mohammadi A, Toumi Z, Zhang Z. The effects of mental fatigue on sport-specific motor performance among team sport athletes: a systematic scoping review. Frontiers in Psychology. 2023;14:1143618.",
   "doi": "10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1143618",
   "abstract": "Scoping review of studies on how mental fatigue affects physical and technical sport-specific performance in team sport athletes. Mental fatigue impaired physical performance, measured as intermittent endurance and total distance, and technical performance in most studies, with small-sided game results more mixed.",
   "tldr": "Mental fatigue from prolonged cognitive tasks tends to reduce endurance and technical skill in team sport athletes, especially in laboratory tests. Effects on small-sided game distance are less consistent.",
   "methods": "Scoping review using the Arksey and O'Malley framework, searching Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EBSCOhost databases and grey literature from March to May 2022. Eligible studies were randomised controlled trials in healthy team-sport athletes that compared a mentally fatiguing task with control and measured sport-specific physical or technical performance. Of 431 records, 18 met criteria at full-text stage, and 16 were retained after QualSyst quality appraisal.",
   "findings": "Eleven studies examined physical performance. Intermittent endurance fell after mental fatigue in several soccer, cricket and Australian football studies (for example, Yo-Yo IR1 distance of 1,203 m vs 1,410 m in one soccer study), while small-sided game distance was unchanged in some studies. Eleven studies examined technical performance, with impairments in ball losses, passing and shooting errors, and tackling in most soccer, basketball and Australian football studies. Perceived exertion rose in most studies that measured it.",
   "limitations": "Only English-language studies were included, and the review covers physical and technical skill but not perceptual-cognitive performance. Study counts are internally inconsistent (12 in the abstract, 16 in the methods and results, 19 in the psychophysiological section), and the number of studies per sport and format is small.",
   "practicalImplications": "Prolonged cognitively demanding work before training or matches may reduce endurance and skill execution, so coaches could plan the timing of cognitive workload around skill and conditioning sessions. The studies used induced fatigue in experiments, so the size of the effect in real competition is unknown.",
   "athleteDev": "Mental fatigue from prolonged cognitive tasks reduced endurance and technical outputs in most team-sport studies, so the timing of cognitive workload before skill or conditioning sessions is worth considering.",
   "rtp": "The review includes only healthy athletes without injury and does not address return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }
}

input.content:
{
 "id": "Q79",
 "sourceFile": "The effects of mobile phone dependence on athletic performance and its mechanisms.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The effects of mobile phone dependence on athletic performance and its mechanisms' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A narrative review of mobile phone dependence (MPD) and athletic performance, drawing on individual and environmental factors, proposed neurobiological mechanisms and psychological theories (general stress, self-determination, compensatory internet use, and uses and gratifications). The authors describe links between MPD and sleep loss, mental fatigue, poorer decision-making and weaker coach-athlete relationships, with the brain reward system proposed as the main mechanism. They present the social cognitive model of self-regulation and the integrative model of self-control as explanatory frameworks.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search method or appraisal of the cited studies is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. Much of the cited evidence concerns acute phone or social-media use or general samples rather than dependence in athletes, and the neurobiological and microwave mechanisms are largely theoretical.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the proposed brain-reward and microwave pathways as established causes of poorer athletic performance, when the review presents them as untested hypotheses.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Mei Z, Zhang Y, Fan Q, Luo S, Luo S. The effects of mobile phone dependence on athletic performance and its mechanisms. Frontiers in Psychology. 2024;15:1391258.",
   "doi": "10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1391258",
   "abstract": "Reviews how mobile phone dependence affects athletes' performance through individual and environmental factors, proposes neurobiological mechanisms centred on the brain reward system, and discusses the social cognitive model of self-regulation and the integrative model of self-control as explanatory frameworks.",
   "tldr": "Mobile phone dependence in athletes is linked to disrupted sleep, mental fatigue, poorer decision-making and weaker coach relationships. Coaches could monitor phone use and build self-regulation and self-control skills, but the mechanisms still need testing.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of previous studies on individual factors, environmental factors, neurobiological mechanisms and theoretical models of MPD and athletic performance. No search strategy is reported.",
   "findings": "Stress and weak self-control may drive heavy phone use, and phone use can impair attention and decision-making. In a volleyball trial, social-media use before training blocked the decision-making improvement seen in controls, and in an eight-week swimming trial, smartphone use before training increased mental fatigue and inhibited performance gains. The review proposes that phone reward cues act on the brain reward system and that microwave radiation may affect dopaminergic circuits, but these links are not directly tested.",
   "limitations": "No search method is reported. The authors note that causal links between MPD and performance are hard to establish, that longitudinal athlete studies are rare, and that the neurobiological mechanisms have not been tested directly in athletes.",
   "practicalImplications": "Coaches could limit phone and social-media use before training, and support athletes in building self-regulation and attention-control skills such as mindfulness. Athletes under stress may need extra attention for signs of problematic phone use.",
   "athleteDev": "Phone use before training may reduce focus, decision-making and training gains. The authors suggest athletes avoid social media for at least two hours before sessions, but the review proposes this and does not test it.",
   "rtp": "The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q80",
 "sourceFile": "The effects of on-field heat index and altitude on concussion assessments and recovery among NCAA athletes.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The Effects of On-Field Heat Index and Altitude on Concussion Assessments and Recovery Among NCAA Athletes' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["American Football", "Soccer", "Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A retrospective cohort of 187 collegiate athletes (71% male) with a documented concussion in competition, drawn from the CARE Consortium, with on-field altitude and heat index reconstructed from weather records and map data. Altitude (median 181 m) was not associated with any acute assessment or recovery outcome (P of 0.265 or more). The authors report that each 1 degree C rise in heat index was associated with shorter symptom recovery (0.05 days, P = 0.047) and clinical recovery (0.14 days, P = 0.006), with R2 values of 0.06 and 0.09.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The design is retrospective, with environmental values estimated from weather databases and maps, and no athletes were injured at true high altitude (2,500 m or more). The Results text gives conflicting heat index coefficients (0.14 vs 0.22 days for clinical recovery, and symptom-recovery P of 0.047 vs 0.114), and a heat index effect on ImPACT reaction time (P = 0.039, Table 3) is not discussed, so the heat index finding is fragile.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the significant heat index results as showing that heat speeds concussion recovery or that heat is harmful, when the authors call the effect too small to matter and it does not appear across all outcomes.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Lempke LB, Lynall RC, Le RK, McCrea M, McAllister T, Schmidt JD. The effects of on-field heat index and altitude on concussion assessments and recovery among NCAA athletes. Sports Medicine. 2020.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s40279-020-01395-5",
   "abstract": "Retrospective cohort of 187 collegiate athletes concussed in competition. On-field altitude did not predict acute assessments or recovery, and higher heat index was associated with shorter symptom and clinical recovery, an effect the authors consider of limited clinical importance.",
   "tldr": "Altitude below 2,500 m at the time of injury does not appear to affect concussion assessments or recovery. Higher on-field heat index was associated with slightly shorter recovery, but the effect is small and not clinically meaningful.",
   "methods": "Retrospective cohort of concussed collegiate athletes from the CARE Consortium (2014 to 2018), restricted to competitions in outdoor sports (n = 187). Heat index, derived from air temperature and humidity, and altitude at the injury location were obtained from Weather Underground and Google Earth Pro. Multiple regression, adjusted for age, sex and concussion history, related these to SCAT, BESS and ImPACT scores under 48 h and to days to symptom and clinical recovery.",
   "findings": "Altitude was not a significant predictor of any outcome (P of 0.265 or more). Each 1 degree C increase in heat index was associated with shorter symptom recovery (0.05 days, P = 0.047; R2 = 0.06) and clinical recovery (0.14 days, P = 0.006; R2 = 0.09). Heat index and altitude did not explain acute SCAT, BESS or ImPACT composite scores (model P of 0.20 or more).",
   "limitations": "The design is observational and retrospective, with small subsets for ImPACT (n = 86) and BESS (n = 99), and no core temperature or acclimatisation data. Travel after competition may have changed conditions, and most events occurred below 500 m. The Results text gives conflicting heat index coefficients, and the heat index effect on ImPACT reaction time is not discussed.",
   "practicalImplications": "On-field altitude below 2,500 m does not need to be factored into concussion assessment or recovery decisions. Heat index may be worth recording, but the authors judge its effect too small to change clinical management.",
   "athleteDev": "The study addresses injury assessment and recovery rather than training or performance, so its relevance for athletic development is limited.",
   "rtp": "Higher heat index at injury was linked to slightly shorter time to symptom and return-to-play clearance, about 0.14 days per degree in the abstract. The effect is small and not clinically meaningful, so it should not be used to set return-to-play timelines."
 }
}
